answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type: databaseAccounts (i.e. Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group (core CLI). Example: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRg --locations regionName=westus2 --kind MongoDB --default-consistency-level Session

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (example: resource cosmos 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: 'myAccount' properties: { databaseAccountOfferType: 'Standard' apiProperties: { serverVersion: '5.0' } } }). Terraform: azurerm_cosmosdb_account (provider azurerm) — resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "myAccount" resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.rg.name location = azurerm_resource_group.rg.location offer_type = "Standard" kind = "MongoDB" mongo_server_version = "5.0" }

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Typical CosmosDB (MongoDB API) connection string: either SRV or standard. Examples: mongodb+srv://<user>:<password>@myaccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/?retryWrites=false&ssl=true (SRV) or mongodb://<user>:<password>@myaccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000. Host suffix: .mongo.cosmos.azure.com. Port (non-SRV TLS): 10255. Required options commonly: ssl=true (or tls=true), replicaSet=globaldb, retryWrites=false.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Azure Cosmos DB (including the MongoDB API on Cosmos) is billed in Request Units (RUs) for throughput. You typically provision RU/s (manual or autoscale) or use serverless where available. There is also an autoscale (RU-based) option; it is not primarily a vCore-based billing model.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: For the MongoDB API you authenticate with database users (username/password / SCRAM). The Cosmos account primary/secondary keys are used for account-level REST/management APIs. Microsoft Entra ID (AAD) RBAC is supported for the Cosmos Core (SQL) management plane, but AAD authentication for MongoDB wire protocol is not generally supported — you should use the MongoDB username/password credentials in the connection string (SCRAM).

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: For an app using the MongoDB API, use standard MongoDB drivers (e.g., the official Node.js driver or Mongoose). There are Azure Cosmos client SDKs (e.g., @azure/cosmos) for the Core (SQL) API, but for MongoDB compatibility you should use the MongoDB driver/Mongoose against the Cosmos-hosted MongoDB endpoint.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: From prior knowledge: Azure Cosmos DB historically did not expose native MongoDB-style vector index types. If vector/ANN is supported it is vendor-specific; there is no standard MongoDB createIndex(...) syntax I can rely on universally. So I would assume vector indexes are not available via a standard db.collection.createIndex call for Cosmos Mongo API. (If the cluster has a vendor extension, its syntax will be documented by that extension.)

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Common approach: integrate Cosmos DB with Azure Cognitive Search for full-text and hybrid search. For simple text queries on the MongoDB API, use MongoDB text indexes (db.collection.createIndex({field:'text'})) if the API version supports them. For richer hybrid search (LLM + vector + text) use Azure Cognitive Search or an external search engine.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: My prior working assumption: Cosmos DB's MongoDB API supports particular MongoDB server versions (commonly 3.6, 4.0, 4.2, 5.0 in various regions historically). Newer wire protocol versions may be added by Microsoft; do not assume 100% parity with the latest MongoDB server release (e.g., 6.x). Commonly missing or partially supported features historically include some aggregation pipeline stages, multi-document ACID transactions or server-side JavaScript, and certain admin commands — check the account's configured MongoDB server version. (Answer uncertain; verify before relying on a specific operator.)

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: For general MongoDB development run the official MongoDB Docker image (e.g., mongo:7.0) and listen on the default port 27017: docker run -p 27017:27017 --name mongo -d mongo:7.0. The Azure Cosmos DB Emulator exists for the Core (SQL) API and runs on ports like 8081 for the REST endpoint, but the emulator historically did not fully emulate the MongoDB API — so for MongoDB-driver testing use a local Mongo image unless you have an emulator that explicitly supports the MongoDB API.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Historically change streams were not supported or were limited on Cosmos DB's MongoDB API. As an alternative you can use the Cosmos DB Change Feed (Core API) for reliable change capture. If change streams are required, validate on the target account whether the configured MongoDB server version and API support change streams before relying on them.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: I do not have a firm prior-memory mapping for "MCP server" tooling. My best guess: the general Azure MCP server used for other Azure data services should cover Cosmos DB operations; there is no separate MCP specifically named DocumentDB beyond standard Azure management tooling. (Low confidence—verify with the environment.)

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: The original name was Azure DocumentDB (the service that provided the Core/SQL API). Microsoft rebranded and expanded it to Azure Cosmos DB. Azure Cosmos DB is Microsoft’s globally distributed multi-model database service; it is not the same as any unrelated open-source project named DocumentDB. The MongoDB API is an additional compatibility surface on top of the Cosmos DB engine.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Underneath is the Cosmos DB proprietary storage/engine with a MongoDB-wire-protocol compatibility layer for the MongoDB API. That means applications use standard MongoDB drivers (same connection string approach), but some server-side features or semantics can differ from a native MongoDB server — you must test and possibly adapt queries and features for Cosmos behaviour.

answers.question: Which environment variable contains the connection string for the live cluster used by this sample?
answers.answer: DOCUMENTDB_URI (read at runtime; do not write the secret anywhere).

answers.question: Which database name should the sample use for all created collections and queries?
answers.answer: Use the database named sample_fintech_12 for everything the sample creates and queries.

answers.question: Which Node.js client library will the sample use to talk to the Mongo-compatible cluster?
answers.answer: Use Mongoose (and the underlying mongodb Node.js driver). Example connection code: await mongoose.connect(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true });

answers.question: What indexes will the sample create to support invoice→PO candidate search (concrete index commands)?
answers.answer: Create compound and text indexes for efficient matching: db.invoices.createIndex({ vendor: 1, amount: 1 }, { name: 'vendor_amount_idx' }); db.invoices.createIndex({ vendor: 'text', description: 'text' }, { name: 'invoices_text_idx' }); For vector-enabled matching (if the cluster supports ANN vectors) create a vector index on the embedding field (vendor-specific syntax). Example optimistic command (vendor-extension syntax) I would try first: db.invoices.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'embedding_hnsw', algorithm: 'hnsw', metric: 'cosine', M: 16, efConstruction: 200 }); — if that fails, fall back to storing embeddings and doing client-side ANN or use the cluster's documented ANN index command.

answers.question: How will the sample connect and authenticate in code (exact line you'd write now)?
answers.answer: In Node.js (Mongoose): const mongoose = require('mongoose'); await mongoose.connect(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true }); // DOCUMENTDB_URI should be the mongodb or mongodb+srv URI with user:pass and TLS options already embedded
